front: What is the **heating value** (calorific value) of a fuel?
back: The energy released when 1 g of the fuel burns completely, in kJ/g.
notes: 1 kJ/g is the same as 1 MJ/kg.

front: How do you calculate a heating value from an experiment?
back: Heating value = energy transferred (kJ) ÷ mass of fuel burnt (g), with energy from q = mcΔT.

front: How do you calculate the efficiency of a stove?
back: Efficiency = useful energy transferred ÷ energy released by the fuel × 100%.
A blue flame; carbon dioxide and water; the most energy released.
A yellow, smoky flame and soot; carbon monoxide (poisonous) forms and less energy is released.

front: Why do ethanol and wood release less energy per gram than hydrocarbons?
back: They already contain oxygen (partly oxidised), which adds mass but releases no energy.

front: Why is damp firewood a poor fuel?
back: Energy is wasted evaporating its water; it burns cooler and smokier.

front: Give three ways to use cooking fuel more efficiently.
back: Use dry fuel, an enclosed or insulated stove, a pot lid and shelter from the wind.

front: Which common fuel has the highest heating value?
back: Hydrogen: about 142 kJ/g (methane about 55, paraffin about 46, charcoal about 30).

front: What decides the cost of the useful heat from a fuel?
back: Its heating value, its price per kilogram and the efficiency of the stove, together.
